articles.summary:
The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement will come into force on October 20, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday.
The two countries had on April 27 signed the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) to boost two-way commerce in goods and services and promote investments.
The agreement will come into force on Dussehra, which is on Oct 20, Goyal said.
The FTA provides duty-free access for 100 per cent of India's exports to New Zealand.
Currently, New Zealand maintains peak tariffs of up to 10 per cent on key Indian goods, including ceramics, carpets, automobiles, and auto components.
New Zealand has committed to invest USD 20 billion over 15 years in India.

articles.summary: The US will extend its online presence review to applicants for I, TN and TD visas from October 1, requiring them to make all their social media profiles public, the State Department said in a notice updated on September 18.The expansion covers foreign media representatives, professionals under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) and their dependants. It adds these applicants to a screening process that already covers several student, worker and exchange visitor visa categories.Also Read| Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee order for another yearWhat are I, TN and TD visas?The I visa is for foreign media representatives travelling temporarily to the US for work, including journalists and people working in radio, film and print. Their activities must involve information or education, generally news gathering and reporting, for a media organisation headquartered outside the US.The TN category allows eligible Canadian and Mexican citizens to work temporarily in specified professional occupations under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Applicants must have a prearranged job and meet the qualifications for their profession. Permanent residence in Canada or Mexico alone does not qualify someone for this category.The TD visa is for spouses and unmarried minor children accompanying or joining a TN professional in the US. Unlike TN eligibility, eligibility as a dependant is not restricted to Canadian and Mexican citizens.What changes from October 1?Applicants for I visas, which cover foreign media representatives, and TN and TD visas, which cover USMCA professionals and their dependants, will face reviews of their online presence.“To support this vetting process, all applicants for I, TD, and TN nonimmigrant visas are instructed to set the privacy settings on all of their social media profiles to ‘public’ or ‘open,’” the department said.The department said it draws on all available sources during visa screening to identify applicants who may be ineligible to enter the US, including those who could pose national security or public safety risks.Which visa categories already face these checks?The screening already applies to F-1 and M-1 student visa applicants and their F-2 and M-2 dependants. It also covers H-1B and H-3 applicants, H-4 dependants of those applicants, and J-1 and J-2 exchange visitors.Other covered categories include A-3 and G-5 visas, along with C-3 applicants who are domestic workers.The existing framework also covers K-1, K-2 and K-3 visas; Q visas for international cultural exchange participants; R-1 and R-2 visas for religious occupations and dependants; and S, T and U categories for witnesses, informants and victims.Also Read| US court blocks Trump administration rule restricting stay for foreign students, journalists“Every visa adjudication is fundamentally a national security decision,” the department said.It said applicants must demonstrate that they qualify for the visa they seek and intend to follow the conditions of their admission. Officials also assess whether applicants intend to harm Americans or threaten US interests.“Receiving a U.S. visa remains a privilege granted at the government's discretion, not an entitlement,” the department said.

articles.title: 3 killed in Pakistani airstrike on Afghanistan
articles.summary: KABUL: At least three people were killed in Pakistani airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday, Afghan officials said, threatening to reignite tensions between the neighbours after nearly three months of relative calm.Relations between the former allies have remained strained since February, when the two sides fought their worst clashes in years.The dispute centres on militancy in Pakistan, with Islamabad accusing Kabul of harbouring militants who stage cross-border attacks from Afghan territory.Afghanistan's Taliban government denies the charges and says militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.The airstrikes on Monday came days after a police facility in northwest Pakistan was attacked, killing at least 16 people.At least one house in Kunar province was hit in the strikes, killing three members of the same family and injuring four others, Taliban deputy spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said in a post on X."In Barmal District of Paktika (province), two locations...were bombarded, destroying one shop and one unoccupied house, with no casualties reported," he said.Pakistan's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Afghanistan had launched drones against Pakistan in July, which Islamabad had said its forces had intercepted and shot down.The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 400 people were killed in a Pakistani airstrike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said targeted a drug rehabilitation centre.Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".Pakistan has a large air force, with 422 combat aircraft and more than 260 helicopters, according to data from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.Afghanistan has no fighter jets but is known to possess at least six aircraft and 23 helicopters, and drones that have previously been used in fighting with Pakistan.

articles.title: SP Group backs Tata Sons listing
articles.summary: Mumbai: The Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) Group is backing a Tata Sons listing after a proposed 2.5% stake sale to monetise part of its holding was delayed, people familiar with the matter said. The SP Group, which owns about 18.37% of Tata Sons, had discussed the sale with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, with a tax-efficient structure involving a bank or financial institution being explored.The proposal stalled at Tata Sons and was formally taken to board only after the RBI's directive brought a listing requirement into focus, the people said.Also Read: Tata’s rival camps lawyer up ahead of looming legal battleThe discussions focused on a limited stake sale rather than an immediate broader monetisation and the proposal envisaged cash proceeds being paid to the SP Group over a defined period, potentially allowing Tata Sons to avoid a listing, the people said. SP Group and Tata Trusts did not comment.The last discussion on the matter with Tata Sons involved Noel Tata suggesting that separate teams from both sides be created to examine the monetisation proposal, the people said. The monetisation plan discussed earlier was being handled by Farokh Subedar on behalf of Tata Trusts, Ankur Verma representing Tata Sons, and a representative from the SP Group, sources said.Also Read: Tata Trusts says Chandrasekaran reappointment resolution was invalid, rejects casting-vote argumentSP Group chairman Shapoor Mistry had publicly backed the listing and said he looked forward to working constructively with Tata Sons on way forward.The SP Group's backing of a listing now gives the conglomerate another potential route to monetise its stake. A public listing could provide a market-based valuation for its holding and make it easier to attract an investor for part of the stake before an IPO, experts said."The SP Group holds just over 18% of Tata Sons and its intent has been to monetise part of this holding in some form," said Ketan Dalal, founder of Katalyst Advisors. "With the IPO now seeming very likely, monetising through an OFS or post IPO, of course, is one possibility." Post-listing lock-in requirements would need to be considered, he said. "Pricing issues would play an important part, both from the investor point of view and from the SP Group point of view. In any case, it is not a situation of one or the other, but it could be a combination of both routes," Dalal said.An earlier proposal in July involved a share swap under which SP Group would receive shares in a basket of listed Tata companies in exchange for part of its Tata Sons holding. Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran had announced in early August that he would not seek reappointment when his term ended in February 2027 and did not participate in subsequent discussions.But he reversed his exit decision and agreed to continue as executive chairman of Tata Sons for another five years after Tata Sons board approved his reappointment on September 17.The SP Group's Tata Sons stake is held through Sterling Investments Corp and Cyrus Investments and has been pledged against borrowings. The group completed a ₹21,500 crore refinancing in July after telling investors it planned to monetise part of its Tata Sons holding through a listing or share sale within 18 months. articles.title: Bengal's industry push needs clear intent
articles.summary: Under BJP, West Bengal is once again debating how to put land together for industry. The debate has now acquired a distinctly technical vocabulary: acquisition, negotiated purchase and land pooling.The three mechanisms are not interchangeable. Acquisition involves compulsory purchase under a statutory framework. Negotiated purchase relies on agreement between landowner and purchaser. Land pooling allows owners to contribute land to a development scheme and receive a smaller, but serviced, and potentially more valuable plot in return. The choice, as recent policy discussions suggest, should depend on the nature of the project.Also Read: Picasso, Omega, Prithvi and Cats: A Mumbai journey through books, unexpected encounters and theatreFor Bengal, the question of land has always been inseparable from the question of industrialisation. So, the new discussion raises a more fundamental question: even if Bengal succeeds in solving the problem of industrial land, will it succeed in attracting capital? Land can be assembled through legislation, negotiation or planning. But capital can only be attracted through confidence.Excitement surrounding political change is understandable. Bengal has always regarded politics not merely as a mechanism of governance but also as a form of public entertainment. Movement of legislators from one camp to another has become a spectator sport.Also Read: Pass the buck to RBI, banks: Let the savings from digital payments fund UPI costs, not consumersCapital, however, follows a different script. It's largely indifferent to the daily theatre of politics, and far more concerned with the stability of institutions. Consider an entrepreneur planning a large investment. The questions are surprisingly simple. Not whether the government is Left, Right or Centre. Not whether ministers speak Bengali, Hindi or English. Not whether people will eat veg or non-veg food. Not whether one political camp will replace another in controlling campuses, institutions or public spaces. The real question is: will rules that exist today survive tomorrow? That confidence in the durability of institutions is what economists and investors describe as institutional credibility.It is in this context that the new government's willingness to reconsider how industrial land is assembled becomes significant. Bengal has already begun examining land pooling, industrial parks, and changes to landholding and land-utilisation rules. The government is also considering ways of making large contiguous parcels available without directly acquiring individual agricultural plots.This is important because Bengal's problem is not simply a shortage of land. It's a shortage of large, contiguous and legally usable parcels of land. Fragmented holdings, overlapping claims and restrictions on land use can make an apparently simple industrial project extraordinarily complicated.134372690Earlier attempts to create land banks from idle public sector land ran into precisely this problem: available parcels were often too small or too fragmented for large investors. Indeed, there are now signs of movement from policy to implementation. The government has cleared land for 33 industries, and that the land will be handed over before Durga Puja. This is significant. But the real test will be whether these allocations translate into timely project execution, employment and sustained private investment.Land pooling could be a useful solution. But it's not a magic wand. Bengal has laws that allow land to be reorganised for development. What matters now is whether these provisions can be implemented effectively, with clear rules on ownership, compensation, infrastructure and land use. Land pooling may bring plots together. But it cannot make ownership disputes disappear.And this is where the land question meets the question of capital. Corruption is costly. But uncertainty can be even more so. Investors can price an unofficial cost. It's much harder to price changing rules, administrative discretion and unpredictable policy.There's also a geographical reality. Large, contiguous parcels are rarely available near Bengal's major cities. So, industry may have to move farther out, where land disputes and infrastructure gaps can be greater. Industrialists, therefore, need to look beyond quick returns and become partners in building these new industrial regions with the government. Given Bengal's political history, industrialisation cannot be reduced to capitalist extraction alone. It must also create a stake for local communities.Capital has no ideology. But it has an excellent memory. Two decades ago, large sections of Bengal's political class mobilised against industrial projects in Singur and Nandigram. Today, many of those political actors either constitute an important part of the new political establishment, or have moved into entirely different political formations.One may celebrate or criticise this phenomenon. But it deserves analysis rather than outrage. The human mind, after all, is a time-variant function. Mathematics teaches us that important variables seldom remain constant. Political preferences are no exception. The objective function of a leader in opposition differs from that of the same leader in government. In electoral democracy, opposition rewards agitation, while government rewards investment; employment and revenue suddenly become governing responsibilities rather than campaign slogans.Consequently, it may be unnecessary to ask whether politicians have become different human beings. The more relevant question is whether the institutional incentives under which they operate have changed.Many of the legal instruments required for assembling industrial land already exist. Creating another set of laws, by itself, will not rebuild West Bengal's industrial land bank. What is required is an unambiguous intention to build industry rather than perform shallow politics. The Left Front came to power in 1977 with a clear intention to pursue land reform for the landless. Today, the era, ideology and people are different. Will the new industrial agenda reflect genuine intent? Or will it be merely political rhetoric?

articles.title: More big names gets SIR notices
articles.summary: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, his wife Kyoko S Jaishankar, CBI Director Praveen Sood and former Army Chief General Upendra Dwivedi are among the prominent people who have received notices from the Election Commission (EC) during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Delhi, according to media reports.Sood's wife Vanita Sood and mother Kamlesh Sood, along with Dwivedi's wife Sunita Dwivedi, have also received notices. The wife and son of CPM MP John Brittas are among those served notices during the exercise.Also Read: Delhi SIR: Advani, Sisodia figure in list of voters with 'discrepancies'The notices have been issued in the New Delhi Assembly constituency.Jaishankar and his wife have been placed in the "unmapped with last SIR" category. This means their current electoral records could not be linked with the rolls prepared during the previous revision exercise in 2002.The couple are registered voters in the Sunder Bagh electoral part of the New Delhi Assembly constituency.Sood, his wife and mother have also received notices under the same category. Dwivedi and his wife have been served notices citing the same discrepancy. They are also registered voters in the New Delhi Assembly constituency.Advani and Sisodia also figured on the listFormer deputy prime minister LK Advani, his daughter Pratibha Advani and daughter-in-law Geetika Advani were among those who received notices during the exercise. Advani's name could not be mapped to the 2002 electoral roll, while his son Jayant cleared the mapping exercise.Also Read: Nagaland's draft electoral roll after SIR retains 11.99 lakh voters, excludes 1.59 lakhFormer Delhi deputy chief minister Manish Sisodia, his wife Seema and son Meer also received notices. Sisodia's notice did not specify the reason, while his wife's notice cited a mismatch in her name and his son's notice referred to a discrepancy in his parent's name.Late economist Bibek Debroy's name appears on notice listThe name of late economist Bibek Debroy, former chairman of the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council, has also appeared on the list of voters flagged for discrepancies during the SIR exercise.Debroy, who was registered as a voter in the New Delhi constituency, died in November 2024. His entry was marked as "unmapped with last SIR".A senior poll officer said officials were aware of his death and that his name would be excluded from the final electoral roll. His name appeared on the list under an EC instruction requiring certain flagged VVIP and VIP entries to be included in the draft roll so that documents could be collected during the claims and objections period.Kejriwal and family members received SIR noticesAAP chief and former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal, his wife Sunita Kejriwal, son Pulkit Kejriwal and parents Gobind Ram Kejriwal and Gita Devi have also received notices during the SIR exercise.The five family members are registered voters in the New Delhi Assembly constituency. Their names were flagged under the "unmapped with last SIR" category, indicating that their current electoral records could not be linked to the rolls prepared during the previous revision.The Electoral Registration Officer said their enumeration forms did not contain sufficient details to establish the required links with the electoral rolls in their respective states.The notices prompted questions from the AAP over why Kejriwal and his family had been flagged during the exercise.Rekha Gupta's name cleared after verificationDelhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta had also received a notice during the SIR exercise after her electoral details were flagged over an age-related discrepancy involving her and her parents.Following verification of her documents and electoral details, her entry was validated for inclusion in the electoral roll for the Shalimar Bagh Assembly constituency.CEO clarifies notices do not mean deletionDelhi Chief Electoral Officer Ashok Kumar has clarified that receiving a notice during the SIR exercise does not mean a voter's name will be deleted from the electoral roll.The CEO's office said no name can be removed without giving the elector an opportunity to be heard and passing a proper, reasoned and appealable order. It added that system-generated notices are being issued to correct data in ECINET.Electors who receive notices can submit their responses and supporting documents to the concerned Electoral Registration Officer or Booth Level Officer. The prescribed list of documents is indicative and not exhaustive, with decisions to be taken on a case-by-case basis.The notice disposal process is scheduled to conclude by October 29, while the final electoral roll is due to be published on November 4.Meanwhile, Delhi received 84,263 Form 6 applications for inclusion in the electoral roll between August 31 and September 19. Another 2,12,400 applications had been received up to August 30. Form 6 is used to apply for inclusion in the voter list.

articles.title: Owaisi open to alliance ahead of UP polls
articles.summary: Lucknow: All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) chief Asaduddin Owaisi on Sunday said that the party is ready to work with those who want to prevent the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) from forming the government in Uttar Pradesh for a third consecutive term, while asserting that the upcoming assembly election in the state will be different from the previous poll.Speaking to about the possibility of an alliance ahead of the UP assembly elections in 2027, Owaisi said that no single party can stop the BJP alone and invited like-minded parties for discussions.Also read: Assembly elections: As polls approach, UP turns into 'katha' pradesh"We do not want the BJP government to be formed for a third time in Uttar Pradesh. If anyone does not want the BJP to form the government, they can talk to us. We are ready to work with you to stop the BJP from coming to power. But it is important to understand that you cannot stop the BJP alone," Owaisi said.Recalling the party's efforts during the Bihar elections, the AIMIM chief said that his party had approached various opposition leaders seeking seats for an alliance, adding that none of them agreed to this."We said this in Bihar as well, and our president, Akhtarul Iman, wrote a letter not just to the RJD or the Congress, but to all the CPI and Communist Party leaders. We said, 'Please give us six seats.' But they did not agree," he said.Owaisi said that AIMIM's organisation has strengthened in Uttar Pradesh and claimed that the party's leadership has emerged from the grassroots level."Our party organisation has become quite strong. Our leadership has emerged at the grassroots level, and our leaders have a strong connection with the ground. The party is working hard on its part," he said.He added that the party would continue its work irrespective of alliance discussions."Whether we are in talks with whom or not is a different matter, but we will continue our work. If you want to stop the BJP, come and talk to us. We are ready to work with you. Now, if they do not want to, that is fine. The people of Uttar Pradesh are watching who wants to stop the BJP and who wants to help it succeed," Owaisi said.Owaisi also said that the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections would not be similar to previous elections and would pose different challenges."Assembly elections are coming. It won't be the 2014 election, nor the 2017 election, nor the 2019 election, nor the 2022 election. This is going to be a completely different election," he said.Targeting the BJP government in Uttar Pradesh, Owaisi alleged that several promises made by the party had not been fulfilled and raised issues related to governance, law and order, electricity and land disputes."This will be a very different election and a very challenging one because the BJP hasn't fulfilled the promises they made," he said.Criticising the previous Samajwadi Party government and the current BJP government, Owaisi said, "When the Samajwadi Party was in power, one kind of hooliganism used to happen. Someone else did it. Now, under their government, a different kind of hooliganism is happening."He also raised questions over the alleged Ram Mandir embezzlement case and sought the release of the SIT report."Why isn't the SIT report released to the public? Why doesn't the government release it? And why are those people getting bail? How are they getting bail? It's strange. This will also be a big talking point," Owaisi said.Talking about AIMIM's preparations for the upcoming elections, Owaisi said that the party has been visiting different constituencies to strengthen its organisation and understand people's issues."In preparation for the upcoming Assembly elections, we have already visited various constituencies in Uttar Pradesh and will continue to do so. Today, we are in Kanpur. In six days, we will be in Shravasti, followed by Azamgarh," he said.He added, "After that, we will hold public meetings in three or four other constituencies in Western Uttar Pradesh. The sole purpose is to strengthen our party organisation for the upcoming elections."Owaisi said that remaining among people helps the party understand their problems on the ground."By staying among the people, we can understand their suffering on the ground and highlight the difficulties this government has created for them," he said.

articles.title: Tata Trusts calls Chandra vote invalid
articles.summary: Tata Trusts has rejected the contention that a casting vote could validate the reappointment of N. Chandrasekaran as chairman of Tata Sons, saying the resolution failed to meet a separate voting requirement under the holding company's articles of association.The Trusts, in a statement on Sunday, said two of their nominees sit on the Tata Sons board and that the articles require affirmative support from a majority of the directors nominated by Tata Trusts, which owns about 66% of the company. One of the two nominees voted against the resolution at the Sept. 17 board meeting, meaning the required support was not secured, it said.Also read: Tata Sons dispute: Abhishek Singhvi says he enters fray with 'sadness and regret'The Trusts disputed the argument that the vote had resulted in a board deadlock that could be resolved by the chairman's casting vote."A condition is either met, or it is not," the Trusts said, arguing that the casting vote applies only when there is an equality of votes at the overall board level and cannot override the separate requirement concerning Tata Trusts' nominees.The Trusts said the resolution to reappoint Chandrasekaran, who has led Tata Sons since 2017, was therefore not validly passed and had no legal effect.The dispute turns on provisions in Tata Sons' articles that give Tata Trusts' nominee directors affirmative voting rights on certain matters. The Trusts said Tata Sons had previously defended those rights before India's Supreme Court during litigation stemming from the removal of former chairman Cyrus Mistry.Tata Sons had argued in that case that the rights were legitimate protections agreed between shareholders and reflected the Trusts' position as the company's majority shareholder, according to the Trusts' statement. The Supreme Court accepted Tata Sons' case and overturned a finding that the provisions were oppressive, the Trusts said.The latest dispute comes as Tata Sons faces renewed scrutiny over its governance and the possibility of a stock-market listing. The Trusts rejected the argument that listing would necessarily strengthen governance, saying Tata Sons had voluntarily adopted several governance practices associated with public companies, including independent directors, audit and nomination committees, related-party transaction rules and insider-trading provisions.Also read: Inside the 24 hours that laid bare Tata’s brutal power struggleThe statement marks a fresh escalation in the disagreement over the governance of India's biggest business group, with the Tata Trusts arguing that the articles themselves provide the framework for resolving the board's decision rather than creating a deadlock requiring intervention by the chairman.The Trusts said their position was rooted in the role they have played in philanthropy for more than 130 years.

of respondents identifying it as the primary benefit.This is followed by stronger employee loyalty at 26 per cent and lower employee attrition at 22 per cent, while 13 per cent see access to untapped talent as the key advantage, it said.According to the report, the manufacturing sector is emerging as one of the biggest beneficiaries of this shift.Around 37 per cent of respondents expect employment expansion."Tier II and III cities are no longer being viewed simply as alternatives to metros; they are increasingly becoming strategic talent markets in their own right.
